name: Weber syndrome
vascularTerritory: PCA/proximal basilar perforators to ventral midbrain, with variable territorial overlap.
presentation: Ipsilateral oculomotor fascicular palsy with contralateral weakness from neighboring descending motor fibers. Pupil involvement and facial/tongue versus limb weakness depend on lesion extent; a nuclear III lesion may have a more complex bilateral/crossed muscle pattern.
cause: Ventral midbrain injury affecting CN III fascicles and cerebral peduncular descending motor pathways, often ischemic but also hemorrhagic or mass-related.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 14, Table 14.9 midbrain syndromes, printed pp. 660 (PDF pp. 686).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 13, third nerve nuclear/fascicular patterns, printed pp. 569-574 (PDF pp. 595-600).

name: Benedikt syndrome
vascularTerritory: PCA/proximal basilar perforators to midbrain basis and tegmentum.
presentation: Ipsilateral third-nerve palsy with contralateral ataxia/tremor or other involuntary movements from crossed cerebellar-output and adjacent tegmental injury. Contralateral weakness may accompany peduncular involvement. These eponymous patterns overlap and exact historical definitions vary.
cause: Midbrain basis/tegmentum injury affecting third-nerve fascicles, crossed superior-cerebellar-peduncle output and variable neighboring structures.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 14, Table 14.9 midbrain syndromes, printed pp. 660 (PDF pp. 686).

name: Claude syndrome
vascularTerritory: PCA/proximal basilar perforators supplying midbrain tegmentum.
presentation: Ipsilateral third-nerve palsy with contralateral ataxia from injury to cerebellar-output fibers above their caudal-midbrain decussation. Prominent weakness is not a defining component but can appear with lesion extension. Historical eponym boundaries vary.
cause: Midbrain tegmental injury involving third-nerve fascicles and post-crossing cerebellar efferents near the red nucleus.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 14, Table 14.9 midbrain syndromes, printed pp. 660 (PDF pp. 686).

name: Nothnagel syndrome
vascularTerritory: A regional dorsal midbrain syndrome, often mass-related; vascular causes have variable PCA/SCA/basilar contributions.
presentation: Historical description of oculomotor dysfunction with cerebellar ataxia from dorsal midbrain/superior cerebellar peduncle-region involvement. Ocular and ataxic laterality can vary with the nuclear, fascicular and crossing structures involved. Contralateral hemianesthesia is not a required defining feature.
cause: Dorsal midbrain mass or other regional lesion affecting ocular motor and cerebellar-output pathways; clinical anatomy is more informative than the variable historical eponym.
refs: Triarhou and Manto, Nothnagel Syndrome, Cerebellum 2023 (online 2022), https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35817948/.
Midbrain infarction causing oculomotor nerve palsy and ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia, 2014, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25224204/.
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 14, warning on historically variable midbrain eponyms, printed pp. 660 (PDF pp. 686).

name: Parinaud syndrome (dorsal midbrain)
vascularTerritory: Dorsal rostral midbrain; often compressive rather than a fixed vascular territory.
presentation: Dorsal midbrain syndrome commonly includes impaired upward gaze, convergence-retraction movements on attempted upgaze, light-near dissociation and lid retraction. Not every feature is present; pupil size, downward gaze and other ocular functions vary.
cause: Pineal-region compression, hydrocephalus, stroke, inflammation or other dorsal midbrain disease. Aqueduct obstruction and the gaze syndrome can coexist, but one does not require the other.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 13, vertical gaze and Parinaud syndrome, printed pp. 587-588 (PDF pp. 613-614).

name: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MLF)
vascularTerritory: MLF injury in pons or midbrain; vascular sources differ with level, including basilar or PCA/proximal basilar perforators.
presentation: During horizontal gaze, the eye on the side of MLF injury has impaired/slowed adduction while the opposite abducting eye often shows nystagmus. Convergence is frequently relatively preserved but is not invariably intact. Bilateral INO can occur.
cause: Disruption of internuclear input from the contralateral abducens nucleus to the ipsilateral medial-rectus oculomotor subnucleus. Causes include demyelination, infarction and other brainstem lesions; age alone does not establish the cause.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 13, INO and horizontal gaze circuitry, printed pp. 585-587 (PDF pp. 611-613).

name: Parkinson's disease
vascularTerritory: Neurodegenerative disease, not a fixed vascular territory; vascular parkinsonism is a distinct differential.
presentation: Parkinson disease produces bradykinesia with rigidity and/or rest tremor; tremor is not obligatory. Gait/postural and nonmotor symptoms vary, and some nonmotor features can precede the motor syndrome. Diagnosis and progression cannot be inferred solely from one atlas structure.
cause: Progressive neurodegeneration prominently affecting nigrostriatal dopamine neurons, alongside wider neural systems and commonly alpha-synuclein pathology. Parkinsonism has several other degenerative, medication-related and vascular causes.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 16, dopamine and Parkinson disease, printed pp. 751-758 (PDF pp. 777-784).
NINDS, Parkinson Disease: Challenges, Progress and Promise, https://www.ninds.nih.gov/current-research/focus-disorders/parkinsons-disease-research/parkinsons-disease-challenges-progress-and-promise.

name: Peduncular hallucinosis
vascularTerritory: Often rostral brainstem or thalamic lesions; causes include posterior circulation ischemia but are not limited to one artery.
presentation: Complex vivid visual hallucinations can accompany midbrain, pontine or thalamic disease, sometimes with sleep disturbance. Insight is often preserved but variable; the content is not necessarily pleasant, and normal cognition/consciousness cannot be assumed in all cases.
cause: Disruption of brainstem/thalamic networks involved in arousal, sleep and visual processing. A proposed release mechanism is not a fully established single-nucleus explanation.
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 14, peduncular hallucinosis, printed pp. 661 (PDF pp. 687).
